questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If no substitution is required, select ‘No substitution’.**

__Being a hot__ and busy day, I felt tired and decided to retire early.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'It being a hot'. **

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence is** 'It being a hot'.**
 
• The expression or the phrase **“Being a hot” **is not the correction expression.
 
• Let us take an example: *“Being a rainy day, he did not go out.”*
 
• The sentence as it stands means that *'he himself is a rainy day'*, which is a logical impossibility.
 
• What the writer wanted to say is *"because it was a rainy day, he did not go out".*
 
• This is **a complex sentence** with one main clause *”he did not go out”* and one subordinate clause *"because it was a rainy day”.*
 
• When converted into a simple sentence, **the subordinate clause** *"because it was a rainy day”* is changed into a phrase, *“it being a rainy day.”*
 
• **Similar rules** can be applied to the given sentence. 
 
• Here, in the given question *'I felt tired and decided to retire early'* is the main clause. And the subordinate clause is *"Because it was a hot and busy day".*
 
• Therefore, as per the points mentioned above, we find that the correct answer is **Option 3. **

**Correct Sentence:__** ***It being a hot** and busy day, I felt tired and decided to retire early. *​

Wait at this billing counter __unless I have bring__ some items I still need to get.

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence is **'until I bring'.** 
 
• Until is a preposition and a conjunction. Until is often shortened to **till or ’til**. **Till and ’til** are more informal and we don’t usually use them in formal writing.
 
• Here, in the given question **'until'** is used as a** conjunction**. 
 
• We use present verb forms to refer to the future after **'until'.** 
 
 
• *Example:*
 
 
• *I can’t wait until the summer holidays begin. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/69a779acc017790d2eea790cc9122762921b180090c4a6901b9133fe30db56bd.png] *
 
• *I can’t wait until the summer holidays will begin. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/b91b169c9a6aba309887b5e1410c56688829831001bc1448ed23f1bec5eca1d8.png] *
 
 
 
 
 
• Here, in the given question** 'have bring'** is incorrectly used. 
 
• Therefore, as per the points mentioned above, we find that the correct answer is **Option 3.** 

**Correct Sentence:__** *Wait at this billing counter **until I bring** some items I still need to get. *​

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/1546db3045588104a59c2dc6b1d15a5e4d651c52124d7bb54bdbc7885c77cea1.png] 

__

• *Example:*

 
 
• *No one left the room until the talk ended. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/69a779acc017790d2eea790cc9122762921b180090c4a6901b9133fe30db56bd.png] *

• Let's use **'until' **as a preposition:

 
 

 **Usage**
 **Example**
 
 

 **Until** as a preposition means ‘up to (the time that)’
 *We played chess until midnight. (up to midnight)*
 
 

 We use from with **until or till** to talk about when something begins and when it ends
 *The road outside our house will be closed from 6 am until 6 pm tomorrow.*
